title: R' Yoshia bar Gizora
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: English translation and editorial notes prepared for Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: He is mentioned at the beginning of [Yerushalmi Shabbat, chapter 3](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Shabbat.3.1.4), as serving Rabbi Zeira. At the beginning of [Taanit, chapter 4](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Taanit.4.1.3), Rabbi Yona says that Yeshua bar Gezora and Rabbi Zeira disagreed. At the beginning of [Midrash Shmuel](https://www.sefaria.org/Midrash_Shmuel.1.1), Rabbi Yona reports in Rabbi Yehoshua bar Gezora’s name: “All silences are bad,” etc.[^1] This saying comes from the end of [Yerushalmi Berakhot](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Berakhot.9.5.19), where the attribution is Rabbi Yona in the name of Rabbi Yosi bar Gezra. Perhaps the name had been abbreviated ר״י and was turned into Rabbi Yosi, whereas it should in fact read Rabbi Yehoshua.[^2]

notes.text: Hyman’s printed page 652 reads כל כרביא בישין, with resh; the existing Hebrew transcription has כדביא, with dalet. The Krakow 1893 edition of Midrash Shmuel 1:1 also reads כרביא and continues with the contrast between ordinary conduct and Torah study. “Silences” follows the explanation of כרבייה in [Ohr LaYesharim on Yerushalmi Berakhot 9:5:19](https://www.sefaria.org/Ohr_LaYesharim_on_Jerusalem_Talmud_Berakhot.9.5.19), which documents both good/bad orders in the Midrash’s textual tradition. Hyman’s printed “bad” is retained here. The Guggenheimer Yerushalmi text instead has כדבייא and the opposite order: ordinary instances are good and those concerning Torah are bad. Penei Moshe proposes reversing that order and explains the word as lying. These differences have not been silently harmonized; the earlier draft’s reference to prophets is unsupported and is withdrawn. The current Hebrew source has not been edited.

רפ״ג and רפ״ד mean the beginning of chapters 3 and 4, not the end. The fetched Shabbat passage names Rabbi Yoshua bar Gizura serving Rabbi Zeira; the Taanit passage names Yoshua bar Gezora and Rabbi Zeura as disputants, confirming the sense of the two men disagreeing with each other and the contextual expansion of ר״ז. The title of the heading remains neutral R'; the other expanded titles have explicit support in the exact named passages. The supplied source’s different forms יושיע, ישוע, יהושע and גיזורה/גזורה/גזורא/גזרא are not merged: the printed page itself has גזורא in its Berakhot attribution, while the Guggenheimer text has Yosi ben Gezira. ר״י remains literal because Hyman is discussing that abbreviation. Hyman’s “perhaps” and his stronger final “should in fact read” remain his differently qualified source-critical claims. The Midrash and Yerushalmi attributions differ as he observes; this does not prove his proposed history of the abbreviation or establish a historical identity.
